Discrete operators encode local geometry and boundary behavior on a mesh. Studying heat diffusion through modes shows how eigenstructure and boundary conditions shape the operator’s behavior.
By the end: Relate mesh operators, boundary conditions and diffusion modes.
Recall question: How do boundary conditions change the modes available to a discrete heat problem?
Heat on a rod: why boundaries, modes, and mesh operators belong together

Take a straight metal rod of length . Its sides are insulated, its ends are held at prescribed temperatures, and someone briefly warms one small region near the middle. The temperature field changes smoothly: the hot spot spreads and its peak falls. We want a model that tells us how the end conditions affect that spreading, how a triangle mesh can approximate it on a curved surface, and what numerical evidence would show that our computation is behaving as intended.
For a uniform rod with no internal heat source, the one-dimensional heat equation is

where is temperature and is thermal diffusivity. For a material with conductivity , density and specific heat capacity , . Conductivity is measured in watts per metre per kelvin, volumetric heat capacity in joules per cubic metre per kelvin, so has units . The second spatial derivative has units temperature per square metre; multiplying by diffusivity gives temperature per second, as required by the left side.

The differential equation describes the interior. It does not specify what the ends do. Those conditions are part of the model, because they determine which temperature patterns can persist and which can appear as independent modes. A simulation without its boundary conditions is an incomplete physical problem.
Boundary conditions choose the modes
First hold both ends at a reference temperature and subtract that reference so the boundary values are zero: . Seek one separable solution . Substitution gives

The left side depends only on time; the right side depends only on position. For the equality to hold for every and , each side must equal one constant. Choose it to be so that the spatial solutions can be oscillatory while the time solutions decay:

The general spatial solution for is . The boundary at forces ; the boundary at then requires . Nonzero solutions exist only when for positive integer . Thus the allowed eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are

and the matching time factor is . A boundary condition has turned a continuum of possible spatial frequencies into a discrete family. The first mode has one broad arch; higher modes have more zero crossings and shorter wavelengths. Their decay rate grows like : fine ripples disappear much faster than broad temperature differences.
The rod’s initial temperature is expanded in this sine family:
Orthogonality makes this projection possible: the integral of the product of two different sine modes over is zero, while the squared norm of each mode is . By linearity, the complete solution is

Each term solves the same PDE and boundary conditions; adding solutions remains a solution because the equation is linear. The coefficients encode the initial pattern; the boundary-selected modes and exponential factors encode how it evolves. The series is not merely a symbolic trick: it says every resolved initial pattern is a weighted sum of independently decaying shapes.

Other endpoint physics changes the spectrum. If the ends are insulated, there is no heat flux through them, so . The spatial modes become for , including a constant mode. That zero mode does not decay: in an insulated rod the average temperature stays fixed. If one end is held at zero and the other insulated, the eigenfunctions are shifted half-wave patterns such as . Robin conditions, which model heat exchange with a surrounding medium, lead to a different eigenvalue equation. Boundary conditions therefore define the operator and its modes together.
The zero mode is not an annoying exception. It carries the conserved average under no-flux conditions. For a uniform rod, integrating the heat equation gives

Insulated endpoints make the right side zero. The rod redistributes heat internally, but its total excess heat—and, for constant heat capacity and cross-section, its spatial average—does not change. Fixed-temperature ends can exchange heat with their reservoirs, so that same integral need not be conserved.
Derivatives act on modes by multiplying their frequency
Why are sine waves so useful? Differentiation does not create a new spatial frequency. For a complex wave ,

A derivative is therefore multiplication by in the frequency representation, and the second derivative is multiplication by . For finite-interval Dirichlet modes, differentiating the sine once gives a cosine, then twice returns the original sine with multiplier . That is exactly the spatial eigenvalue relation . The heat equation consequently becomes a separate scalar decay equation for every mode: .

This makes the “high frequencies decay faster” statement precise. If the initial temperature contains only a low mode and a high mode, after elapsed time their amplitudes are multiplied by . When the high mode has four times the wavenumber, it has sixteen times the decay exponent. Smoothing is thus a low-pass operation. It removes oscillations because second derivatives penalize rapid spatial variation.

A Fourier series describes periodic patterns; a sine expansion on can be understood by extending a function oddly outside the interval and then periodically. A cosine expansion corresponds to an even extension. The chosen extension matters at the endpoints. If the interior initial temperature does not agree with the fixed end values at , the odd periodic extension has a jump. The series still represents the interior in a limiting sense, but convergence near that jump oscillates. This is one way that boundary assumptions show up as ringing rather than disappearing behind the algebra.
From a mesh Laplacian to a heat operator

The mesh-topology spine introduced a cotangent Laplacian for vertex values. We can now give it a clear evolution meaning. Let be a temperature stored at mesh vertex . Build a stiffness matrix from the surface geometry and a mass matrix from the areas represented by the vertices. For a common cotangent convention, each interior edge has weight . Set off the diagonal and choose . Then is symmetric and, for a suitable mesh, positive semidefinite. A lumped mass matrix is diagonal with , a local area; a consistent finite-element mass matrix can include off-diagonal terms.
With this positive stiffness convention, the discrete heat equation is

If the previous mesh note uses , this is the same statement . Signs vary across libraries, so test the constant field and a known mode before wiring a new matrix into an update. For a constant vector , every edge difference vanishes, giving when there is no imposed-temperature boundary. Thus an isolated closed surface or natural no-flux boundary has a zero mode, just like the insulated rod.

The mass matrix is not bookkeeping overhead. It turns an integrated stiffness balance into a rate per unit area or length. On a triangulated surface, has units square metres and cotangent entries in are dimensionless; therefore has units inverse square metres. Multiplying by surface diffusivity in square metres per second gives a rate in inverse seconds. In a one-dimensional finite-element rod, the mass entries instead have units metres and the stiffness entries have units inverse metres, so still has units inverse square metres. The matrix dimensions depend on the domain dimension, but the discrete operator approximating a second spatial derivative always carries inverse-length-squared units.

Under a coordinate scaling by factor , areas on a surface scale as while cotangent weights are invariant. Thus scales as . The diffusivity must be expressed in the same physical length units as the geometry. A mesh stored in millimetres paired with in square metres per second is inconsistent until one representation is converted. Dimensional checks catch this error even when every number in the code looks plausible.
The generalized eigenproblem

is the mesh counterpart of the rod’s spatial mode equation. Its eigenvectors are discrete temperature patterns; its eigenvalues measure how rapidly each pattern bends across the surface. The evolution of a mode amplitude is . Because is symmetric and is positive definite, these modes can be chosen orthogonal in the mass-weighted inner product . This is the finite-dimensional version of the orthogonality that made the sine-series coefficients independent.

It requires a linear solve, and a large step can still erase detail or be inaccurate even though it does not blow up. Stability and fidelity are different questions.

On a 2D mesh with area mass matrix, the explicit stability limit is controlled by a largest eigenvalue of order , where is a representative edge length. Refining edge length by two can therefore require roughly four times as many explicit steps for the same simulated duration. This cost is one reason implicit diffusion is attractive in geometry processing. It does not follow that every mesh flow should be implicit: intended feature behavior, accuracy, solver conditioning and cost still matter.
A Green function is an impulse response

A Green function answers a concrete experiment: what field is produced by a unit point source, subject to the same boundaries as the original problem? For a linear operator with homogeneous boundary conditions, define by
where the subscript reminds us that differentiates in the observation coordinate . A distributed source is a superposition of point sources, so the solution is
For time-dependent heat flow, the impulse response depends on elapsed time. With the rod’s normalized Dirichlet eigenfunctions , the heat kernel is

A point of heat inserted at spreads according to ; an initial field evolves as . A time-varying source contributes through a space-time convolution, integrating over earlier times and source positions . This is the continuous analogue of repeatedly applying a linear diffusion update to source inputs.

The kernel is symmetric in and for a self-adjoint diffusion operator with the same homogeneous boundary conditions on both arguments. In the rod case this follows term by term because each factor is . More generally, Green-function reciprocity follows from self-adjointness and the boundary terms vanishing under the chosen domain and boundary conditions. If coefficients, boundary conditions, or the operator make the problem non-self-adjoint, do not assume . For a weighted Sturm–Liouville problem, symmetry may be with respect to the appropriate weighted inner product or measure rather than plain coordinate integration.

There is a subtle zero-mode case. With insulated boundaries, the Laplacian has a constant eigenfunction with eigenvalue zero. The steady Poisson equation with pure Neumann conditions cannot have a solution for arbitrary nonzero-mean : integrating both sides shows the source must satisfy the net-flux compatibility condition. Even when compatible, the solution is defined only up to an added constant until a mean or reference value is fixed. The transient heat kernel remains meaningful; the zero mode simply preserves the average instead of decaying. A numerical inverse that silently divides by a zero eigenvalue is not a valid Green-function construction.
Sampling, truncation, and ringing

A continuous field becomes finite data only after sampling. On a regular 1D grid, the highest alternating mode is near the Nyquist frequency, roughly one half-cycle per sample spacing. Shorter wavelengths cannot be represented uniquely: they alias into lower-frequency patterns. On irregular triangle meshes there is no single global Nyquist number, but local edge length and element shape limit which oscillations are resolved. If the initial hot spot is narrower than the sampling scale, the mesh may miss its peak or encode it as a misleading pattern. Subsequent heat flow smooths the samples it received; it cannot reconstruct the lost sub-grid event.

A truncated Fourier or eigenfunction sum introduces another approximation. Keeping only the first modes reconstructs the broad structure well when the field is smooth, but a sharp jump needs many modes. Near a discontinuity, partial sums can overshoot and oscillate (Gibbs behavior); increasing narrows the affected region but does not remove the limiting overshoot at the jump. In heat flow, each mode is additionally multiplied by an exponential decay. At positive time, high-frequency terms are strongly damped, but at time zero the series must still represent the initial/boundary data correctly. If initial temperature and fixed endpoint temperatures disagree at a corner in space-time, a rapid boundary layer is physically implied, not a failure of the series method.

For a finite mesh, eigenvalue truncation and timestep are separate resolution controls. Dropping small-scale eigenvectors discards spatial detail; taking a large implicit-Euler step changes each mode’s decay relative to the continuous evolution (its factor exceeds for ); taking an unstable explicit step amplifies the highest modes. A visually smooth result is not proof of accuracy because excessive smoothing can hide aliasing, poor mesh quality, or a wrong boundary condition. Report sample spacing, kept modes or timestep, and error against a known field when making a quantitative claim.
Manufactured fields make the solver testable
A manufactured solution gives an analytic answer for a problem with known boundaries and coefficients. For fixed-zero endpoints choose one sine mode
It satisfies both the PDE and . With , , and , the center temperature is

For a second, independently decaying mode at twice the wavenumber, the decay exponent is four times larger. A two-mode initial field tests that the solver handles superposition and does not accidentally mix modes in a uniform rod with homogeneous endpoints. Compare grid values to the analytic field at fixed physical times while halving and reducing consistently; measure error rather than relying on a plot.
For a no-flux test choose

Its derivative is zero at and , and its spatial mean is at every time. A discrete solver should preserve the corresponding mass-weighted mean up to rounding and linear-solver tolerance. For fixed-temperature endpoints, instead measure boundary flux. Fourier’s law gives heat flux ; integrating the temperature equation yields the net heat change from inflow at one boundary minus outflow at the other. The rod’s interior energy need not be conserved when reservoirs hold its ends at fixed temperature.

On the mesh, the matching tests are: for a no-flux/closed setting; symmetry ; nonnegative generalized eigenvalues; exponential decay of each measured eigenmode at rate ; and conservation of when no heat crosses the boundary and no source is present. For Dirichlet vertices fixed to a reservoir, remove or constrain those degrees of freedom and verify the change in total heat matches integrated boundary flux. A matrix can be symmetric and still have the wrong units, scale, boundary rows, or source signs, so keep the analytic rod and unit checks beside the structural matrix checks.

The rod story now carries through to a curved triangle mesh. Material and boundary conditions define a differential operator; its self-adjoint eigenmodes form a basis; spatial derivatives multiply modes by their squared frequencies; the mesh stiffness and mass matrices approximate that operator; and time integration advances its modes according to their decay rates. Green functions express how localized heat sources propagate under those same boundaries. Sampling and truncation set what detail can be represented, while manufactured solutions and flux balances tell us whether the computed field matches the stated model.
What the boundary means to the discrete solver

Boundary data must be encoded in the discrete unknowns and matrix, not merely displayed as a condition in a comment. With fixed-temperature Dirichlet endpoints, the endpoint values are known and are removed from the unknown vector or incorporated into the right-hand side. If a known endpoint value is nonzero, its neighboring stencil contains a source contribution proportional to that value. A common error is to drop the endpoint neighbor term when constructing the reduced matrix, thereby solving a different rod with an insulated or shortened boundary.

For an insulated endpoint, the Neumann condition says the normal heat flux vanishes. A finite-volume view writes heat balance in terms of fluxes through cell faces; the boundary face contributes zero flux. A finite-difference view can use a ghost value reflected across the endpoint, such as , so the centered derivative is zero. Either construction should leave the constant vector in the nullspace and conserve the weighted sum. Dirichlet and Neumann are not interchangeable “edge handling” options: one couples the rod to a reservoir; the other isolates it.

For a curved mesh, an open boundary has an analogous choice. A natural finite-element boundary on the diffusion problem usually represents zero flux unless a boundary term is supplied. Pinning boundary temperatures imposes a Dirichlet constraint. A Robin boundary can represent transfer to an ambient temperature, with flux proportional to the difference between the surface temperature and ambient. If the application actually intends a heat bath but the implementation leaves the natural no-flux condition, total mesh heat will be conserved incorrectly. Boundary semantics are part of the physics API.
Self-adjointness explains why a clean mode decomposition exists. For the one-dimensional operator with homogeneous Dirichlet conditions, integration by parts gives

The boundary term vanishes because both functions are zero at each end. For homogeneous Neumann conditions, it vanishes because both derivatives are zero. Other boundary conditions may also yield a self-adjoint operator, but this must be checked rather than assumed. The eigenvalues are real, distinct-eigenvalue modes are orthogonal, and the operator can be diagonalized in that basis. This is the continuum reason the heat equation reduces to independent exponential decays.
The same fact has a discrete energy witness. If is symmetric positive semidefinite and is positive definite, then

This quadratic norm is not the total heat; it measures squared temperature variation around the chosen zero reference. It decreases under diffusion. Total heat in the no-flux case is instead , and it stays constant because . Keeping these two quantities separate prevents the false claim that “heat is conserved” means every norm or every boundary case is conserved.
Spatial and temporal error have different signatures
For a smooth sine mode with wavenumber , the centered difference approximates the second derivative by the discrete eigenvalue

The leading error is proportional to for a fixed resolved mode. Since is slightly less than at small but finite , the discrete mode decays a little more slowly than the continuum mode. Near the grid’s highest frequency, the approximation is no longer close to ; the grid cannot represent finer structure. This is spatial discretization error, distinct from the forward-Euler time error and its stability limit.

A convergence experiment should separate them. Fix a smooth analytic initial field, hold temporal error small while refining , and compare at a fixed time to estimate spatial convergence. Then fix a sufficiently fine spatial grid and reduce to measure temporal convergence. Finally sweep the ratio toward the stability edge to verify the predicted highest-mode amplification. If both and change arbitrarily in one experiment, a smaller error cannot be attributed to either change.
A practical manufactured solution can include a source term as well. Choose a smooth field satisfying the desired boundary values, then define

The field is now an exact solution of by construction. For example, let , whose endpoints remain zero. Differentiate it analytically to construct . This tests the source assembly, boundary treatment, spatial operator and time stepping together without needing a complicated closed-form solution to an unrelated physical problem. Report a normed error, such as , at stated times.

The mode formulas also support an impulse-response check. A sharply localized initial heat pulse can be projected onto the sine basis; its coefficient for mode is the pulse’s inner product with . At later times, each coefficient must be multiplied by . Compare direct time stepping against this truncated spectral reference on a fine grid. The two methods will not match exactly because one has grid and timestep error and the other has truncation error, but their discrepancy should shrink under the declared refinements. This test exercises the same linear evolution from two independent representations.

For a self-adjoint problem with a zero Neumann mode, the steady Green function for an inverse Laplacian is singular because constants are annihilated. One must project out the constant mode, enforce a zero-mean source, and choose a gauge such as zero-mean solution. For the transient heat kernel, the constant mode is retained: it is the long-time average left after all nonconstant modes decay. This distinction matters in mesh processing too. Solving a Poisson equation for geometry may need a pinned vertex or mean constraint; evolving heat on a closed surface should generally preserve the mean rather than accidentally delete it.

The continuous and discrete models therefore have matching but not identical contracts. In the continuum, the boundary condition defines the operator domain and Green identity. In the mesh, it determines constrained rows, boundary flux terms and the nullspace. In the spectrum, it selects modes and eigenvalues. In the time step, it controls stability and decay. Verifying one layer with the appropriate witness makes it possible to localize a bad result instead of compensating for it with an arbitrary damping factor or a smaller timestep.
PDEs, fields, and discrete solvers
Fields and PDEs express spatial behavior; discretization and boundary conditions determine the numerical system.
PDE discretization and variational structure

A partial differential equation includes derivatives along several spatial axes. The 2D Laplacian is . A regular-grid finite difference approximates each second derivative from neighboring samples. On a mesh, a discrete Laplace operator uses connectivity and geometry weights. The heat equation moves a value toward neighboring values; the wave equation uses acceleration proportional to spatial curvature. Boundary conditions affect the solution everywhere because waves or diffusion interact with the boundary.

Explicit diffusion on a grid has a stability limit roughly proportional to , where is grid spacing and diffusivity. Refining the grid by two can require about four times smaller time steps in 2D explicit schemes, rapidly increasing cost. Implicit discretization leads to a sparse linear system. Matrix sparsity reflects local neighborhood connectivity; numerical linear algebra is therefore part of the simulation pipeline.
Optimization connects to PDEs through energy minimization. A continuous energy functional is stationary when it satisfies the Euler-Lagrange condition

After discretization, the field becomes a finite vector and the functional becomes a finite objective. Its gradient can be minimized with the same methods used for curve fitting. The continuum equation and discrete optimizer are two views of one problem. CMU-22 · CMU-23
The same field equation can describe very different behavior

A PDE describes a field whose value depends on location and time . The derivatives say how the field changes. For a ripple height, is vertical displacement at each point of a pond. For heat, it is temperature at each point of a surface. For smoke, it might be velocity, density, or vorticity. The equation is an implicit rule: it constrains the field, but the field must still be computed from initial data, boundary data, and a numerical method.

The Laplacian is , the divergence of the gradient. Equivalently in Cartesian coordinates it is the sum of second derivatives, in 2D. A useful intuition is “difference from the local average”: it is near zero where the field matches its neighborhood and large where the field has a local bump or dip. The coordinate formula looks tied to axes, but the Laplacian itself is unchanged under a rigid rotation of coordinates.
Three equations provide contrasting mental models:

The Laplace equation is elliptic. With boundary values fixed, it finds a harmonic field that smoothly interpolates them. The heat equation is parabolic: an initial temperature distribution spreads and smooths; at steady state, , so it becomes the Laplace equation. Diffusion also acts as a model of damping or viscosity. The wave equation is hyperbolic: an initial bump propagates as a wave rather than simply disappearing. This matters numerically, because wave errors can travel for a long time instead of being averaged away. Burgers’ equation, , adds a nonlinear transport term and a diffusion term; transport can steepen a wave toward a shock while diffusion softens it. A PDE is linear when the unknown field and its derivatives appear linearly; products such as or nonlinear functions of make it nonlinear. Its order is the highest derivative order present. CMU-23
Discretize the space with a representation that fits

Finite differences replace derivatives by differences of samples. For equally spaced 1D samples separated by spacing , the centered approximation to the second derivative follows by differencing neighboring first slopes:
In a regular 2D grid with equal horizontal and vertical spacing, the five-point Laplacian is

The center has weight and each immediate neighbor has weight . The numerator is the sum of neighbor values minus four times the center value. It measures local non-flatness and gives a simple update for ripples or heat diffusion.

A grid is an Eulerian representation: values are stored at fixed spatial locations while material passes through them. A Lagrangian representation follows particles or mesh vertices as they move. Particle methods adapt naturally to moving material and unbounded domains, but a good particle distribution is difficult to maintain and local derivative estimates require neighbor searches. Fixed grids have regular, cache-friendly operations and straightforward finite differences, but they impose a domain and a resolution; fine features blur or alias when the grid is coarse. Hybrid methods such as FLIP, material point methods, and particle level sets mix moving samples with fixed grids to keep useful properties from both.
On a triangle mesh, the cotangent Laplacian replaces grid-neighbor weights with geometry-dependent weights. For scalar values at mesh vertices, a common unnormalized form is

where is the set of vertices connected to , and are the two angles opposite edge . Implementations may divide by a local area or mass matrix, so normalization conventions must be checked. On a regular triangulated grid, the cotangent construction agrees with the familiar grid stencil up to its chosen scale. The lesson is broader than this one formula: express the spatial operator in a representation appropriate to the problem, and the same time integrator can often be reused across a grid, a mesh, or a hybrid domain. Boundary data is part of the equation

The Laplace equation alone does not determine a unique interpolated field. A constant is harmonic because its Laplacian is zero; indeed, on a periodic grid with no fixed values, both the all-zero field and every constant field solve . To define an interesting solution, state what happens at the boundary.

Dirichlet boundary conditions fix the value of the field, such as temperature around a plate or height around a domain. Neumann conditions fix the derivative in the outward normal direction, , which is related to heat or fluid flux across the boundary. Robin conditions prescribe a linear combination of value and normal derivative. These choices are physically meaningful: fixed temperature, insulated boundary, or exchange with an environment are different problems.

Boundary values and derivatives cannot always be chosen independently. In 1D, a harmonic function satisfies , so it is a line . Any pair of endpoint values determines a line, but two endpoint slope conditions must agree because a line has one slope. In a 2D harmonic Neumann problem, the divergence theorem gives a compatibility condition. Integrating the normal derivative around the boundary equals integrating over the interior. Since , the net boundary flux must be zero:

Even with compatible flux, adding a constant leaves both the Laplacian and normal derivatives unchanged, so one value or a mean-value constraint must be fixed to choose a unique representative. This is a simple example of a well-posedness check: verify a solution exists and is sufficiently determined before trusting a numerical solver. After solving a linear system , compute the residual ; a large residual may reveal a bad setup or incompatible boundary data, not merely a weak solver. CMU-23
Turn the discretized equations into a solver

For a grid Laplace problem, the equation at each interior cell says that its value equals the average of its four neighbors. Repeatedly replacing each value with that average is Jacobi iteration. It eventually spreads boundary information inward, but it is slow on large grids: distant parts of the domain communicate only through many neighbor-to-neighbor updates. Instead, assign a single index to every unknown grid value and assemble all local equations into one matrix system . Each row has a small number of nonzero entries because each cell couples only to nearby cells. The resulting matrix is sparse; use a sparse linear solver rather than storing and multiplying all the zeros in a dense matrix.
For heat diffusion, explicit Euler updates the current field using the current Laplacian:

Each cell moves toward the neighborhood average. But explicit diffusion is conditionally stable: for a regular grid the safe step scales like . Halving the grid spacing can require about four times as many time steps in 2D, making fine grids expensive. An implicit step evaluates the diffusion at the new field and solves a sparse linear system; it allows larger stable steps at the cost of a solve.

The wave equation has a second time derivative. It can be rewritten with a velocity field as two first-order equations, and . Alternatively, a centered second difference uses two previous time slices:

This needs an initial displacement and initial velocity (or two compatible initial frames). The spatial Laplacian may be the grid stencil or a cotangent mesh operator. The same time-stepping code can therefore propagate a ripple on a regular grid or waves over a triangle mesh, provided the boundary and operator are correctly specified. A low-resolution thin-shell wave can also be upsampled with Loop subdivision for an interactive visual result; interpolation adds surface detail, but it does not replace the underlying simulation. Discrete field equations and their stability conditions
From a PDE to a sparse system and a stable update

A partial differential equation (PDE) constrains a function that varies over space, time, or both. A numerical method must choose (1) what values represent the field, (2) how to approximate spatial derivatives, (3) how to advance in time if time is present, and (4) what boundary behavior is imposed. The same physical equation can therefore produce different algorithms on a fixed grid and on a moving triangle mesh. The examples below use the Laplace and heat equations to make each choice explicit. CMU-23 (PDF pp. 30–46; video 00:36:00–00:54:00)

Poisson and Laplace equations become sparse linear systems
The Poisson equation is , where is a prescribed source field. Laplace’s equation is the special case . For the common positive-diagonal matrix convention, multiply the stencil by :

This equation has one row for each unknown grid value. Each row touches only the center and its four immediate neighbors, so the matrix has mostly zeros: it is sparse. Number the unknown cells from to , put the center coefficient on the diagonal, put in a neighbor’s column for each grid neighbor, and put zero elsewhere. The right side holds plus contributions from any known boundary values. Then solve with a sparse linear solver. If instead one defines the matrix to approximate directly, its diagonal is negative and neighbor coefficients positive; both conventions are equivalent if the right side and signs are changed consistently.
For example, take one unknown interior cell with spacing , zero on all four neighboring boundary cells, and constant source . The Poisson equation becomes

so . The positive-diagonal form gives , the same answer. For a source-free Laplace cell with fixed neighbor values , the equation is , hence . The harmonic value is exactly the average of the four neighbors. The second trace is the local equation that Jacobi iteration applies: replace each unknown with its neighbor average, repeat, and allow boundary data to propagate inward. Jacobi is simple but may converge slowly on large grids because distant locations communicate only through repeated local updates. A sparse solve attacks all equations together. Boundary conditions are part of the mathematical problem, not a software afterthought. Dirichlet data fixes the field value at the boundary, such as a prescribed temperature. In matrix assembly, substitute that known value into the adjacent interior equation and move its contribution to the right-hand side; the boundary value is not an unknown. Neumann data fixes the derivative along the outward normal, which represents a flux. It changes the boundary stencil or supplies a flux contribution. Robin data combines a value and a normal derivative. Periodic wraparound is another choice: a neighbor on the right edge is identified with a cell on the left edge.
For a harmonic solution with Neumann boundary data, the net prescribed flux must be zero. Integrate over the domain and apply the divergence theorem:

Here is the 2D region, is area measure, is its boundary, is boundary length measure, and is the outward unit normal. Thus inward and outward flux must balance. There is a second issue: adding a constant to a harmonic function leaves its derivatives and Neumann data unchanged. The solution is therefore only defined up to a constant unless one value or the average is pinned. In a linear system this appears as a nullspace (a nonzero vector mapped to zero). Check compatibility and constrain the nullspace before solving. Afterward, compute the residual ; its norm measures how closely the computed vector satisfies the assembled equations. A small residual cannot prove the boundary model is correct, but a large residual can reveal an incompatible or poorly solved system. CMU-23 (PDF pp. 36–43; video 00:49:00–00:58:00)
Explicit heat flow and its stability limit

The heat equation is . The symbol means change of the field per unit time; is thermal diffusivity, controlling how quickly heat spreads. Forward Euler estimates the time derivative by , where is a time-step index and is the time interval. Combine it with the five-point stencil. With equal grid spacing in both directions, define . Then

Every superscript denotes the old time, and denotes the new time. The center’s resulting coefficient is ; each neighbor’s coefficient is . If , all five coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one. The update is then a weighted local average, which avoids making a new value overshoot the current local range for this diffusion stencil. The first lecture also sets the scope of the subject. Horn describes the course as physics-based machine vision: rays travel through a lens, light interacts with a surface, and measurements follow from that image-formation process. The lecture then removes the patent’s eight-direction quantization in two ways. First, choose the two sampling points directly along the measured gradient direction and interpolate their brightness from the pixel grid. One-dimensional linear interpolation suffices along that line; cubic interpolation can use more samples for a smoother estimate. This puts the suppression and peak fit on the true normal direction and eliminates the later plane-position correction. It also makes sample spacing vary continuously, so the calibration curve must account for a continuum of distances; interpolation error itself matters at -pixel targets. Second, sample at a fixed radius around the candidate point. The three samples then have a consistent physical spacing for every gradient direction, but off-grid values require two-dimensional interpolation. Bilinear interpolation is cheap but less accurate; bicubic interpolation uses a wider neighborhood (roughly a support) and costs more. The patent’s quantized design is therefore a deliberate balance between geometric consistency, interpolation error, memory, and arithmetic. MITV-12 (video 01:08:43–01:17:40)

The lecture also reviews how CORDIC turns Cartesian gradient components into magnitude and angle. Conceptually, rotate the vector until its vertical component is near zero; the accumulated rotation angle is the direction and the final horizontal component approximates the magnitude. General rotations require sine, cosine, and four multiplications. CORDIC chooses a sequence of progressively smaller angles . Then and are close to powers of two, so multiplication becomes a bit shift; each step uses shifts and additions/subtractions, and accepts the sign that reduces the remaining vertical component. The fixed gain from the sequence of rotations is precomputed and corrected if absolute magnitude matters. First inspect signs and swap axes as needed to bring the vector into the first octant; then vectoring iterations converge rapidly. This explains both CORDIC’s historical appeal in fire-control computers and why the best choice depends on whether a modern chip’s multipliers or memory lookups are cheaper. Hough voting turns weak local evidence into a global hypothesis

The classical Hough transform was motivated by bubble-chamber photographs. A particle track appears as separated bubbles of unequal size and spacing, so ordinary edge linking cannot reliably trace one continuous contour. For a line , each observed point constrains possible parameters by —a line in slope-intercept parameter space. Every bubble votes along its parameter-space line; bubbles belonging to the same physical track produce votes that intersect near one common . An accumulator array bins those votes, and peaks identify likely lines. One noisy point does not say which line is correct; it reduces the possibilities to a one-dimensional family. MITV-14 (video 00:53:31–01:06:25)

The same construction generalizes. If a circle’s radius is known, a point says the center must lie on the circle in center-parameter space. The LTE time-advance example gives an intuitive ranging analogue: a measured round-trip delay fixes a phone-to-tower distance, so the unknown tower lies on a circle around that phone position; several measurements accumulate evidence at their common center. If radius is unknown too, the parameters form a three-dimensional space, and each measured point votes for a cone of possible circles. Noise spreads votes across neighboring bins, but a good hypothesis still collects more evidence than alternatives. The cost is that quantizing a high-dimensional parameter space requires a large accumulator, so Hough voting is most useful when local evidence is incomplete and the global parameterization is compact. Recognition, templates, and industrial matching
Recognition compares image evidence against transformed templates, choosing scores and search spaces suited to expected variation.
Industrial recognition: templates, transforms, and tolerances

Industrial machine vision often has a known object family, controlled lighting, and a need for reliable pose measurement. This is a different setting from unconstrained semantic classification. A binary template or edge template stores geometric evidence from a reference object. At runtime, the system searches for a transformation that aligns template evidence with image evidence. Normalized correlation compensates for scale/offset changes in measured intensity, while edge-based matching can be less sensitive to uniform brightness shifts. MITV-13 (notes pp. 73–78)

The course begins this topic with a careful contrast between raw image correlation and gradient-based matching. For template image and runtime image , minimizing the squared difference is equivalent to maximizing cross-correlation when the two self-energy terms do not vary with translation. A first-order Taylor expansion for small shift leads back to the brightness-constancy flow residual. This makes local optical flow a small-displacement approximation to template alignment. Correlation handles larger translation searches directly, but global occlusion or missing object regions can badly affect the score. Mean subtraction removes intensity offset; dividing by the norms yields a normalized correlation that is less sensitive to contrast scaling. It still cannot make an occluded region informative. MITV-13 (notes pp. 74–76)

PatQuick is presented in the lectures as a fast, robust multidimensional object-detection and pose method. The key perspective is geometric: detection means finding a location and transformation whose predicted template features agree with measured features. Its industrial focus makes repeatability, inspection tolerances, and computational cost central. The method’s patent title is “Method for Fast, Robust, Multidimensional Object Detection and Pose Determination” (US 7,016,539), as named by the course. MITV-13 · MITV-14

PatQuick does not need to keep and rescan a full template image at every possible pose. Its training stage finds boundary points, connects neighbors with consistent directions into chains, removes short or weak chains, splits chains near high-curvature corners, and places evenly spaced probes along retained low-curvature segments. It stores probe positions, gradient directions, weights, pattern contrast, and a selectable granularity that defines the resolution below which image variation becomes unresolved. Probe points can lie between pixels. At runtime, transformed probes sample only selected image locations; the system accumulates their direction or magnitude agreement into a multidimensional score surface. A peak in that surface proposes object pose. This sparse evidence design trades exhaustive pixel comparison for a compact model, but its accuracy remains limited by pose-space quantization and probe placement. MITV-13 · MITV-14 (notes pp. 75–80)

The pose search spans translation, rotation, scale, skew, and aspect ratio. In the lecture’s generalized affine view, and encode six independent 2-D affine degrees of freedom. More degrees of freedom make the match family more expressive while causing the configuration count to grow rapidly at fixed quantization. Coarse-to-fine search is therefore a computational strategy, not just a display convenience: coarse levels find candidate basins; finer levels spend effort where evidence supports a match. The notes describe hexagonal sampling and peak detection for translation; a hexagonal neighborhood improves spatial sampling efficiency over a square grid for comparable resolution, with tie-breaking rules needed to avoid ambiguous peaks. MITV-14 (notes pp. 78–81)

Scoring itself has a statistical interpretation. Random background texture can coincidentally provide a probe gradient in the expected direction. The course computes a baseline random-match contribution and discusses subtracting it, rather than treating any high raw score as meaningful. Direction matching is often more robust than gradient magnitude because magnitude changes with contrast and lighting; magnitude can still be used with saturation and weights. Normalized scores cost more but reduce dependence on the number or strength of probes; raw weighted scores are cheaper for fine scanning after a coarse candidate is already found. The system also compensates for whether a transformation changes gradient direction: pure translation, rotation, and uniform scale preserve it, while shear and aspect-ratio changes transform isophote orientation. MITV-14 (notes pp. 78–81)

The Hough transform handles noisy or incomplete local evidence by letting each observation vote for global parameter values consistent with it. For example, an edge pixel with a known normal may vote for line parameters; peaks in an accumulator indicate parameter combinations supported by many pixels. This trades direct combinatorial search for a discretized parameter-space histogram. Resolution matters: coarse bins merge distinct hypotheses; fine bins increase memory and sensitivity to noise.

A homography is a projective matrix that maps homogeneous image coordinates between views of a plane: , where is a nonzero scale and are three-component homogeneous coordinates. It can represent planar perspective changes, but a single homography does not describe arbitrary 3-D scenes with parallax. Multi-scale search reduces cost by locating a candidate at a coarse resolution before refining translation, scale, or orientation at finer levels. MITV-14 (notes pp. 78–84)

PatMax is another industrial alignment method emphasized through distance fields. Given template edges, compute for each image location the distance to the nearest observed edge (or an equivalent signed/unsigned distance representation). A transformed template can then be scored by summing those distances at its expected edge points. This makes small edge localization errors degrade the score smoothly instead of causing a hard pixel mismatch. The method still depends on sensible edge extraction, a good transform search, and a tolerance appropriate to the inspection task. It is not invariant to arbitrary deformation; the allowable transformations encode what “same part, different pose” means. MITV-15 (notes pp. 84–93)

PatMax is specifically positioned as a refinement stage after PatQuick. PatQuick searches a quantized pose space broadly and can start without an initial estimate; PatMax assumes an approximate pose and iteratively improves it without quantizing pose space, enabling subpixel refinement. Its training data include edge fragments and a vector field that attracts runtime edge evidence toward the template field. Unlike the earlier direction-quantized pipeline, PatMax avoids CORDIC and quantized gradient directions when high precision is the goal. A mechanical-spring analogy is more accurate than literal electrostatics: runtime dipoles experience forces, and a small set of allowed pose changes turns those forces into parameter updates. A 2-D translation contributes two degrees of freedom, rotation one, and scale one; affine refinement can add skew and aspect effects for six degrees total. Local linearization yields a weighted least-squares update, accumulated efficiently, but no general closed-form answer exists for all edge configurations. The cascade is therefore coarse global capture followed by local, continuous optimization. MITV-15 (notes pp. 84–89)

The Cognex-style model replaces the full image patch with a sparse set of probes. Training begins from a clean golden sample, computes and links subpixel boundary points, splits chains at sharp curvature changes, then redistributes probe locations to a chosen density. Each probe stores a position, expected gradient direction, and weight; the model also stores a useful coarsest granularity and expected contrast polarity. Runtime matching transforms the small model onto the precomputed gradient image and samples only at probe positions. That is efficient because a model may contain tens or hundreds of probes instead of millions of pixels. The runtime image remains untouched: transforming a few model coordinates is cheaper and avoids resampling or rotating the entire image. MITV-13 (video 00:27:43–00:31:51, 00:34:35–00:40:53, 00:47:18–00:48:39)

The direction of an edge gradient is generally more stable than its magnitude when illumination or material response changes. A direction score can therefore be flat within a tolerance and decline linearly outside it: the example accepts errors through fully, fades to zero by , then wraps around the full circle. If the application permits contrast reversal, an additional acceptance lobe near is needed. That doubles the angular range in which unrelated edges can count as partial matches, so polarity invariance increases false evidence. If gradient magnitude is used, it can be ignored, used as a weight, or scored with saturation so very strong gradients do not dominate without bound. Summing weighted probe evidence over a pose gives a score surface; search peaks propose instances, while an end-stage threshold accepts or rejects each one. Weak edge fragments are retained through early stages and rejected only when they form too short or low-total-weight chains, postponing a fragile threshold until evidence accumulates. This representation also accommodates inspection. A probe with negative weight can penalize an expected edge that should be absent, such as the continuation of a rounded phone outline beyond its endpoint. Such probes can disambiguate a symmetric shape, but unlike positive probes extracted automatically from an edge chain, the negative ones require human-authored knowledge and were described as uncommon in automated use. A missing or occluded part lowers match score rather than necessarily destroying the match, allowing the same alignment to support defect inspection. A CAD outline can generate a model, but a real golden sample may be better when fabrication rounds corners or distorts the ideal design. MITV-13 (video 00:41:04–00:43:23, 01:05:57–01:10:40)

The search space is built from application-relevant degrees of freedom: image translations, cyclic rotation, logarithmic size change, and—only when the optics or object pose require it—shear and independent axis/aspect changes. A percentage size increment is better expressed logarithmically: a fixed increment in log scale yields a similar percentage change for small and large objects. Every added degree of freedom increases cost, so omit unsupported transformations. Search begins on coarse quantized pose grids, using efficient hexagon-centered translation patterns and tie-breaking rules for hexagonal neighborhoods, then refines around promising candidates with finer steps. Multiple local candidates should be kept because an early coarse peak may not be the global match. The approach is a strong initializer for a later continuous optimizer, but its final precision is limited by the pose-grid spacing. MITV-13 (video 00:53:03–01:01:53, 01:17:56–01:23:00)

The patent makes its abstraction explicit by defining “image,” “brightness,” “boundary,” “granularity,” “model,” “training,” and “pose,” even extending “image” beyond visible-light photographs to simulated data or quantities such as height and temperature. For computer vision, the useful lesson is that a detector’s model should state what evidence is stored, at what spatial scale, and which transformations count as the same object. The lecture’s older parallel-binary methods remain useful after another computation has already produced a reliable mask: connected components provide area, perimeter, centroid, and Euler number (components minus holes). Applying them directly to natural scenes requires thresholding too early, while sparse gradient probes retain graded evidence until the full pose score is assembled. PatMax: continuous pose refinement after coarse localization

PatQuick and PatMax solve complementary search problems. PatQuick makes a sparse probe model and searches a quantized pose space broadly enough to produce an initial match. PatMax assumes that initial pose lies in the correct capture basin, then iteratively improves position and orientation by minimizing a weighted least-squares-like alignment energy. The patent calls an update an attraction step and prefers four iterations as a practical stopping rule; a different system can stop when the update or residual is small. Because it never globally explores all poses, PatMax can refine more precisely but can converge to the wrong local match if initialization is too far away. MITV-15 (video 00:00:12–00:06:59, 00:31:45–00:36:57)

Training computes subpixel edge fragments from the golden image. PatMax calls these oriented fragments dipoles, but the course cautions that the name suggests the wrong physics: point charges or electric dipoles have singular or orientation-dependent interactions, unlike this algorithm. A mechanical spring analogy is closer. Imagine each runtime edge sample connected to the nearest compatible training edge by a spring; alignment reduces total spring energy. Since an edge measurement constrains position mainly across its normal and is ambiguous along its tangent, the target end should slide along the model edge like a carriage, rather than attach to an arbitrary point. MITV-15 (video 00:02:16–00:04:13, 00:24:16–00:25:22)

The model stores both oriented edge fragments and a dense two-dimensional attraction field. Field vectors encode distance and direction back toward nearby trained edges, but only out to a chosen cutoff. Beyond that, the cell is marked unknown so distant texture cannot provide misleading attraction. Propagation begins at known subpixel boundary seeds, then fills neighboring cells outward. Manhattan distance is simple to update exactly with axis steps but is not Euclidean; Euclidean distance requires more careful geometry, especially when each cell stores a direction vector as well as a length. Where fronts from two edge segments collide, similar proposals can be combined, but a large disagreement indicates a corner; mark the region so it cannot spuriously pull the alignment. This is a directed distance field, not merely a scalar distance transform. MITV-15 (video 00:13:22–00:24:15, 00:41:18–00:45:14)

At runtime, PatMax detects edges in the live image, maps those comparatively few dipoles back into the precomputed model field, and aggregates their local forces. This reverses PatQuick’s mapping direction: PatQuick moves a small trained model over a runtime gradient image; PatMax moves runtime edge samples through a trained field. In either case the whole image is not warped at every candidate pose. Translation follows the vector sum . Rotation follows torque about a chosen center, , where the planar cross product contributes only its out-of-plane scalar. Scale can be estimated from radial forces, because a size mismatch stretches the spring-like displacements more strongly farther from the center. The chosen transformation parameters are coupled, so these sums form a local linearized least-squares system; solving it yields one update, not a closed-form global optimum. MITV-15 (video 00:25:25–00:31:26, 00:45:17–00:48:44)

The dense field and candidate edges support inspection in two directions. Coverage asks what fraction of trained model boundaries found a runtime match; clutter asks how much runtime edge evidence is unexplained by the trained object. A missing gear tooth can preserve a good pose but reduce coverage. An extra scratch or textured background can increase clutter. These metrics make positioning, recognition, and part inspection distinct outputs of one matcher. A client map first corrects rectangular or unequal camera pixel pitch so calculations occur in a Cartesian square grid. Multiscale training builds a separate model at each resolution: refine at a coarse level for speed, then use that pose to initialize finer edge geometry. MITV-15 (video 00:07:04–00:12:38, 00:27:22–00:28:34, 00:31:27–00:36:57, 00:40:11–00:41:15)
C. How should an edge alignment score behave?

A raw binary overlap score changes abruptly when a predicted edge moves by one pixel. A distance-field score changes gradually: each transformed template point receives a penalty based on its distance to the nearest observed edge. That smoothness supports optimization and tolerance to quantization. However, overly broad distance penalties can let an incorrect nearby contour score well; the distance scale should reflect the inspection tolerance and expected edge uncertainty. MITV-15
